system.name: Circinus X-1
system.description: One of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, 9,400 light-years away in Circinus. A neutron star and an evolved giant companion trace a highly elliptical orbit every 16.6 days; at closest approach the neutron star tears away mass in intense X-ray bursts, while relativistic jets stream outward at near-light speed — all inside a supernova remnant only ~4,600 years old.

cirx1-ns.name: Circinus X-1
cirx1-ns.description: A young neutron star — possibly a magnetar — formed in a supernova whose remnant is still visible as a radio shell surrounding the system. At each periastron, when the companion swings within 0.14 AU, tidal forces drive supercritical accretion onto the neutron star surface, detonating thermonuclear Type I X-ray bursts bright enough to be seen across tens of thousands of light-years.
cirx1-ns.funFact: Circinus X-1 sits inside a radio supernova remnant estimated to be only about 4,600 years old — making it one of the youngest known X-ray binaries, and giving astronomers a rare view of a neutron star within centuries of its birth.

cirx1-companion.name: Circinus X-1 Companion
cirx1-companion.description: A late O-type or early B-type giant of roughly 7 solar masses. Its highly elliptical orbit sweeps between 0.14 AU (periastron) and 0.38 AU (apoapsis) from the neutron star, creating a dramatic range of X-ray brightness throughout the orbit. At periastron Roche-lobe overflow drives intense accretion; at apoapsis the system fades almost to quiescence.
cirx1-companion.funFact: The extreme orbital eccentricity is almost certainly a relic of the supernova kick — the asymmetric explosion that birthed the neutron star imparted a velocity kick that distorted what was probably once a circular orbit into this elongated path.
